Approach chosen by the product owner: squashed baseline. supabase/migrations/ now holds one file, 20260806000005_squashed_baseline.sql — the converged schema the previous 89 produce, taken with pg_dump --schema-only --schema=public from a real three-pass build. userStories.title: Pin search_path on SECURITY DEFINER functions
userStories.description: 50 SECURITY DEFINER functions do not pin search_path. A SECURITY DEFINER function without a pinned search_path can be tricked into resolving an unqualified name against an attacker-controlled schema.
acceptanceCriteria: Every SECURITY DEFINER function in the public schema declares SET search_path
The search_path check in scripts/verify-schema.mjs is promoted from a note to a blocking check
npm run verify:schema passes
The lead pipeline smoke test still passes, confirming no function broke
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-06 in migration 20260806000003_pin_security_definer_search_path.sql. All 50 pinned via ALTER FUNCTION rather than rewriting bodies, so there is no chance of a transcription error in the logic and the migration is idempotent for the CI three-pass loop. Pin is `public, extensions, pg_temp`, not bare `public`: pgcrypto and uuid-ossp live in `extensions` both locally and on hosted Supabase, and generate_encryption_key() calls gen_random_bytes(), so a bare public pin would have broken it -- confirmed by calling it after the pin. pg_temp is named last precisely so it is searched last instead of first, which is the actual attack. The two functions already pinned (search_path=public and search_path=public, auth) were left alone. Demonstrated both ways on a clone of log_audit_event: unpinned, an authenticated attacker's `CREATE TEMP TABLE audit_logs` captured the audit row (temp=1, real=0) -- the audit trail silently diverted; pinned, the same attack captured nothing and the row reached the real table (temp=0, real=1). The search_path check in verify-schema.mjs is promoted from a note to blocking check 8, proven to fire by unpinning one function (exit 1) and restoring it (exit 0). Verified on a from-scratch three-pass rebuild: 146 tables, all 8 checks pass including the lead pipeline smoke test, validate-migrations passes on 88 files, and types.ts is still in sync.

userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-06. Crypto moved into a new `pii-crypto` Edge Function holding PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY; src/lib/pii.ts is now a thin client that cannot decrypt anything on its own, which is the point. VITE_PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY is gone from src/lib/pii.ts, .env.example and DEPLOYMENT.md's env table. Existing ciphertext survives: supabase/functions/_shared/encryption.ts already produced a byte-identical envelope to the old client (same enc:v1: prefix, PBKDF2-SHA256 at 100k iterations, 16-byte salt prepended to the 12-byte IV, base64-of-JSON), verified by reading both implementations side by side. So the migration is carrying the key across, not re-keying -- DEPLOYMENT.md §2.1 documents setting the function secret to the current VITE_PII_ENCRYPTION_KEY value, then removing it from Cloudflare Pages. Rotation is written up as a separate job needing a decrypt-old/re-encrypt-new backfill, and is the reason the plaintext columns should not retire until after it. Batched rather than per-value, or the leads list would have been two round trips per row: pii.ts gains encryptPIIBatch/decryptPIIBatch, useLeads decrypts a whole page in two calls and encrypts both fields in one, and values needing no work (empty, or lacking the enc:v1: prefix) short-circuit locally so an all-plaintext page makes no request at all. The function requires a JWT and is rate limited per user rather than per IP (agents behind one office NAT should not share a budget); confirmed check_rate_limit takes p_identifier text so a `user:<uuid>` key works. Encrypt fails closed, decrypt fails open. Found and removed an adjacent instance of the same defect while checking for leftovers: src/hooks/useEncryption.ts had zero callers and read VITE_ENCRYPTION_SECRET with a hardcoded fallback default -- another bundled key, one import away from being picked up. Deleted along with its env var. src/lib/encryption.ts is kept (pure primitives that take the secret as an argument and read no env var, plus its tests guard the envelope the edge function must stay compatible with) with a header note saying so. pii.test.ts rewritten against a stubbed edge function, covering position preservation, the local short-circuits, and both failure directions: 14 tests, suite total 274 -> 277. tsc unchanged at 321, eslint 0 errors, build and verify:schema green.

userStories.title: Unauthenticated SSRF in seven URL-fetching edge functions
userStories.description: crawl-site, check-broken-links, check-security-headers, detect-redirect-chains, analyze-images, check-core-web-vitals and check-mobile-first all take a caller-supplied URL, pass it through new URL() — which parses, it does not validate — and fetch it. No scheme check, no private-range or link-local block, no allow-list. http://169.254.169.254/ and http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ are both reachable, from a process holding the service-role key, with the response body returned to the caller. _shared/url-validation.ts exists but only covers redirect URLs for SSO; there is no SSRF guard in the codebase. All seven are also unauthenticated (US-078).
acceptanceCriteria: A shared guard in _shared/ rejects any URL that is not http/https, resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or unique-local address, or names a metadata endpoint
The guard resolves DNS and checks the resolved address, so a hostname pointing at 127.0.0.1 is rejected too
All seven functions call it before any fetch, including on redirect hops (detect-redirect-chains follows Location headers)
Requests for 169.254.169.254, 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8 and a public hostname with a private A record are all rejected — verified by executing the functions
A legitimate public URL still crawls successfully
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. New supabase/functions/_shared/ssrf-guard.ts, wired into all seven. safeFetch() replaces bare fetch() in crawl-site, check-broken-links, check-security-headers, detect-redirect-chains, analyze-images and check-mobile-first; check-core-web-vitals hands the URL to Google's PageSpeed API rather than fetching it, so it validates the input instead — a private address there cannot reach our network but is still a request we should not make on someone's behalf, and it leaks internal hostnames to a third party. The guard blocks non-http(s) schemes, localhost/.internal, and the private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, multicast and reserved ranges — and, importantly, RESOLVES the hostname and checks the answer, because internal.example.com with an A record of 10.0.0.5 defeats any string check. It re-checks every redirect hop, since a public URL that 302s to 127.0.0.1 defeats a single up-front check. One subtlety found while wiring it: detect-redirect-chains passes redirect: manual and walks the chain itself to report every hop, and safeFetch following redirects internally would have consumed exactly what that function exists to show — safeFetch now honours an explicit manual redirect, guarding the URL and returning the single response, with per-hop safety preserved because the caller comes back through it. 6 tests cover the address matching, including IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:127.0.0.1) and the ranges either side of the private blocks (172.15/172.32, 192.167/192.169) so an over-broad prefix check would fail. Running them needed vitest.config.ts extended to include supabase/functions/**/*.test.ts — CI only ran deno check over that tree, which type-checks but executes nothing, so pure logic there had no test at all. RESIDUAL, NOT CLOSED: DNS rebinding. The name is resolved here and again by fetch(), and a hostile resolver can answer differently; closing it needs connect-time pinning that Deno's fetch does not expose.

userStories.title: Stripe hardening: real rate limiting, durable idempotency, and a fail-closed plan default
userStories.description: Three defects in the billing path. (1) There are two rate limiters: _shared/rate-limiter.ts is DB-backed via rpc('check_rate_limit'), _shared/rateLimit.ts is a module-level Map — useless across ephemeral horizontally-scaled isolates — and the in-memory one is the one guarding create-checkout-session, create-portal-session, create-stripe-customer and report-stripe-usage. (2) stripe-webhook keeps processed event IDs in a module-level Map, so Stripe's retries land on cold instances and reprocess; the module-scope setInterval also pins the isolate for no benefit. (3) getPlanNameFromPriceId ends `return priceMap[priceId] || 'professional'` and the result feeds getPlanLimits, so any price ID not in the hardcoded map or the STRIPE_PRICE_* env vars silently grants professional entitlements.
acceptanceCriteria: The four Stripe functions use the DB-backed limiter and _shared/rateLimit.ts is deleted
Webhook idempotency is persisted in a table keyed on the Stripe event id, with the unique violation as the check
Replaying the same webhook event twice against a cold instance processes it once — verified by executing it
An unrecognised price ID resolves to 'free', not 'professional', and is logged as an error
The module-scope setInterval is removed
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000009_stripe_webhook_idempotency.sql plus the five functions. (1) All four Stripe endpoints moved off _shared/rateLimit.ts onto the DB-backed checkRateLimitDb, and rateLimit.ts is deleted — it was a module-level Map, so it reset on every cold start and never saw a sibling isolate's counts, meaning the money endpoints had the one limiter in the codebase that did not work. rate-limiter.ts gained a getRateLimitHeaders matching the old helper so the swap did not change any response shape. (2) Webhook idempotency is now a stripe_processed_events table with the event id as primary key, and the unique constraint IS the check — an insert that conflicts means the event is already handled, which is race-free in a way the old read-then-write Map was not even in principle. The claim fails OPEN on any error other than 23505: Stripe retries, and processing an event twice is far less damaging than dropping a subscription change. The module-scope setInterval sweeper is gone with it. (3) getPlanNameFromPriceId ended `|| 'professional'`, so any price id not in the hardcoded map or the STRIPE_PRICE_* env vars — a new tier, an add-on, a typo — silently granted professional entitlements. It now falls back to 'free' and logs the unrecognised id as an error; entitlement defaults fail closed. Verified against a rebuilt Postgres: the first claim inserts, a replay is rejected with 23505, one row remains. RECORDED, NOT FIXED: billing state is still split across subscriptions (flat, with the limit columns, read by useSubscriptionLimits) and user_subscriptions (relational, read by checkout/portal). stripe-webhook dual-writes both consistently across all five event types so it works today, but two sources of truth kept in sync by one function is a standing hazard and deserves its own story.

userStories.title: Adopt native Supabase MFA so the second factor is enforced in the token, not the client
userStories.description: signInWithPassword completes and issues a full session before any second factor is considered (useAuthStore.ts:318-377). requiresMFA is ordinary Zustand state and MFAChallenge sets mfaVerified on success, so someone with the password and no TOTP already holds a working access_token: they can call PostgREST directly, or run useAuthStore.setState({ mfaVerified: true }). Separately SecureRoute's requireMFA prop is a no-op because getSecurityContext hardcodes isMFAVerified = true (authentication.ts:196-207, comment: 'For now, assume verified if they got past login').
acceptanceCriteria: MFA uses Supabase's native enrol/challenge/verify so that the second factor determines the session's AAL
A user with MFA enabled who has not completed the challenge cannot read their own leads via a direct PostgREST call — verified by executing it with the pre-challenge token
RLS on at least the lead and subscription tables requires aal2 for MFA-enrolled users
getSecurityContext reports real MFA state rather than a hardcoded true, and SecureRoute's requireMFA prop does something
Existing enrolled users are migrated or re-enrolled without being locked out
npm run test:run still passes
userStories.notes: This is the largest story in this batch and it touches every enrolled user. The custom setup-mfa/verify-mfa/disable-mfa functions and the user_mfa_settings, mfa_trusted_devices, mfa_temp_codes and mfa_verification_logs tables all become redundant or need repointing — plan the migration path for already-enrolled users before writing code. Do not ship a half-migration that leaves both systems live.

userStories.title: PII encryption on leads is defence-in-depth theatre
userStories.description: leads.encrypted_email and encrypted_phone are dual-written by useLeads.ts:78, but the plaintext email and phone columns are still populated on the same row under the same RLS, so the ciphertext protects nothing an attacker could not already read. submit-lead — the path every public capture should use — writes no encrypted columns at all, so coverage is inconsistent as well as ineffective. gdpr-export/index.ts:174 already carries a TODO to decrypt on read.
acceptanceCriteria: Either the plaintext columns are dropped and every reader decrypts (useLeads already has the read path), or the encrypted columns are dropped and the feature stops being described as encryption at rest
Whichever direction is chosen is applied consistently across useLeads, submit-lead and gdpr-export
Existing rows are backfilled or migrated, not left in a mixed state
gdpr-export returns readable contact details for the data subject
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: Dropping the plaintext is the only version of this that provides real protection, but it means every query that filters or sorts on email/phone has to change, and search over encrypted columns is not free. If the cost is too high, choose the honest option and remove the encryption claim from the docs rather than leaving both.

userStories.title: Analytics fabricates its comparison period, so every trend reads +17.6%
userStories.description: AnalyticsDashboard.tsx:57-60 builds the previous period as Math.round(stats.totalViews * 0.85) with the comment 'Estimate 15% growth'. Every trend arrow on /dashboard/analytics-advanced therefore reads a constant +17.6% regardless of what happened, including during a decline. revenue and avgResponseTime are hardcoded 0 in the same object and flow into the KPI cards.
acceptanceCriteria: The previous period comes from a real query over the preceding window
A period with fewer views than the one before it renders a negative trend
revenue and avgResponseTime are either computed or removed from the KPI cards rather than displayed as 0
npm run test:run and npm run build still pass
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. useAnalytics now queries the preceding window of the same length and returns previousStats, replacing AnalyticsDashboard's `Math.round(stats.totalViews * 0.85)` with the comment "Estimate 15% growth" — which made every trend arrow read a constant +17.6% regardless of what happened, including during a decline, when it showed growth. The previous-window query selects only what it counts rather than pulling another 1,500 rows to length them. Also returns hasPreviousPeriod, and the dashboard now says so explicitly when there is no prior data instead of rendering a meaningless +100%. The two hardcoded zeros were handled differently because they are different problems: avgResponseTime IS computable — leads.first_responded_at exists — so it is now the mean minutes to first response over responded leads, null when none have been; revenue is not tracked anywhere in the product, so the Revenue KPI was removed from calculateKPIs rather than left rendering $0 beside real numbers, which reads as "you earned nothing" rather than "not measured". analytics.test.ts updated to expect 7 metrics and to assert Revenue is absent. tsc 147 -> 143 across this batch, 295 tests, build green.

userStories.title: Fix the keywords admin policies — they error for everyone, including admins
userStories.description: The three keywords write policies use EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM auth.users WHERE users.id = auth.uid() AND users.raw_user_meta_data->>'role' = 'admin'). Policies are evaluated with the caller's privileges and authenticated has no grant on auth.users, so the check raises — verified: ERROR: permission denied for table users. Keyword management is therefore broken for admins too. Separately, raw_user_meta_data is user-writable via auth.updateUser({ data: … }), so if that grant ever appeared any user could self-declare role: admin.
acceptanceCriteria: The three policies use has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin'::app_role) like the other 270-odd policies
An admin can insert, update and delete keywords — verified by executing it as an admin
A non-admin cannot, and a non-admin who sets raw_user_meta_data.role = 'admin' still cannot
No RLS policy in the public schema references auth.users directly (see US-082)
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000003_fix_keywords_admin_policies.sql. The three write policies now use has_role(auth.uid(), 'admin'::app_role) TO authenticated, matching the ~270 other policies. Verified on a rebuilt Postgres: an admin can insert, update and delete; a non-admin is rejected with "new row violates row-level security policy" on insert, and their UPDATE and DELETE affect 0 rows. The non-admin used in the test has raw_user_meta_data set to {"role":"admin"} — the exact escalation the old policy would have permitted had the auth.users grant ever existed — and is still denied. anon still reads active keywords. Worth recording how nearly this was mis-verified: the first test run reported "UNEXPECTEDLY ALLOWED" for the non-admin insert, which was an artefact of psql continuing past a failed statement without ON_ERROR_STOP and printing the trailing SELECT anyway. The same trap produced a false "SELF-GRANT SUCCEEDED" during the original review. Always set ON_ERROR_STOP when a test asserts that something is denied.

As anon, seo_core_web_vitals and seo_keyword_history return 0 rows
As a freshly registered non-admin user, every table in this story returns 0 rows
The SEO admin dashboards still work as an admin

userStories.title: Clear the 1 critical and 21 high dependency advisories
userStories.description: npm audit reports 1 critical and 21 high. jspdf (path traversal, PDF/JS injection, several DoS) is the critical. react-router and @remix-run/router carry an open-redirect-to-XSS chain and are on every user-facing path. Also high: axios, vite, postcss, sharp, ws, lodash, form-data, brace-expansion, minimatch, nanoid, js-yaml, jws, glob, flatted, fast-uri, picomatch.
acceptanceCriteria: react-router/react-router-dom and jspdf are upgraded to non-vulnerable versions first
npm audit reports 0 critical and 0 high, or each remaining advisory has a recorded reason it is not exploitable here
npm run build, npm run test:run and npm run test:a11y still pass after the upgrades
Routing, PDF export and image handling are exercised manually after the upgrade
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. 27 advisories (1 critical, 21 high) -> 2 moderate. Two passes. First, npm audit fix --package-lock-only took 27 -> 6 without touching package.json: that alone cleared react-router/@remix-run/router (the open-redirect-to-XSS chain, and the one on every user-facing path), axios, vite, postcss, ws, lodash, form-data, brace-expansion, minimatch, nanoid, js-yaml, jws, glob, flatted, fast-uri and picomatch. Then three major bumps for the rest: jspdf 2.5 -> 4.2 (the critical: path traversal, PDF/JS injection, several DoS), jspdf-autotable 3.8 -> 5.0, sharp 0.34 -> 0.35. Remaining 2 moderate are react-router/react-router-dom with no fix published. Major bumps of a rendering library are not verified by a typecheck, so src/lib/exportUtils.test.ts was added to actually drive it: a table export, a full report (summary cards, autotable, footer, landscape, grid theme) and CSV. Writing it was worth it twice over — the first draft failed with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading map)", which looked like an API break in autotable v5 and was actually my test passing a metrics/tables shape that PDFReportOptions has never accepted (it takes headers/rows/summary). The real code needed no changes for either major bump. sharp is declared in package.json but imported nowhere in src/ or scripts/ — worth removing outright in a follow-up.

userStories.title: Cleanup: dead code, a broken admin widget, and forgeable analytics
userStories.description: Three small items from the 2026-08 review that do not warrant their own stories. src/components/dashboard/LinkManager.tsx is dead code — nothing imports it; it keeps links in React state, never calls Supabase, toasts 'Link added successfully!' and models a schema (link, type, up_link, click_number, numeric id) that does not match the links table, while useLinks.ts is the real implementation. HealthDashboard.tsx:135 selects user_subscriptions.plan_name, a column that does not exist on that table, so the widget 400s. analytics_views carries FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true) with no TO clause, so anyone can inflate any profile's view analytics.
acceptanceCriteria: src/components/dashboard/LinkManager.tsx is deleted
The HealthDashboard subscription widget queries real columns and renders
analytics_views inserts are rate limited, and the profile view counters are documented as untrusted or derived from a source that is not anonymously forgeable
npm run build passes and the tsc count does not rise
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08. All three items. LinkManager.tsx deleted (US-081 commit), HealthDashboard fixed (US-082 commit), and analytics_views now throttled by migration 20260808000010. The open anonymous INSERT stays — this is a public link-in-bio, visitors have no session, and view tracking has to work for them — but it is now bounded: a BEFORE INSERT trigger caps 30 views per minute per (visitor, profile), silently dropping over-limit rows via RETURN NULL rather than raising, since a rejected view must not surface as an error on a visitor page and the client insert is fire-and-forget. A trigger rather than an edge function because the insert goes straight from the browser to PostgREST and moving it would change the tracking path for every profile. Two mistakes worth recording. First, the trigger called check_rate_limit as though it returned a boolean; it RETURNS TABLE(allowed, remaining, reset_at), so every insert failed with "argument of NOT must be type boolean, not type record" — and the verification then read "0 recorded", which looked exactly like a working throttle. Second, after fixing that, the count still read 0 because the verification query ran as anon and analytics_views SELECT is scoped to auth.uid() = user_id — anon cannot read back what it just wrote. Re-checked as the owner: 50 forged views from one visitor -> 30 recorded, a different visitor unaffected. HONEST LIMIT: visitor_id comes from localStorage and is trivially rotated, so this raises the cost of inflation rather than preventing it. The counters should be treated as indicative.

userStories.title: Account deletion fails outright, and would orphan tenant data if it did not
userStories.description: Found while verifying US-083. process_scheduled_account_deletions() performs DELETE FROM auth.users, which raises: insert or update on table "audit_logs" violates foreign key constraint "audit_logs_actor_id_fkey". The chain is: deleting auth.users cascades to profiles (FK ON DELETE CASCADE) -> the audit_profiles_changes trigger fires -> audit_table_change calls log_audit_event with p_actor_id => auth.uid(), which is NULL under the cron/service-role caller, so log_audit_event COALESCEs it to the user being deleted -> that INSERT references an auth.users row already removed in the same statement -> FK violation -> the whole DELETE aborts. ON DELETE SET NULL on audit_logs does not help because the row is being inserted, not updated. So a GDPR right-to-erasure request is accepted, scheduled, the 30-day grace period elapses, and the job then errors forever. Separately, even once the delete succeeds it would not erase much: leads, listings, testimonials, user_settings, article_webhooks and analytics_views have no foreign key on user_id at all, so nothing cascades to them. Those rows carry lead names, emails and phone numbers.
acceptanceCriteria: DELETE FROM auth.users for a provisioned account succeeds — verified by executing it, not by reading the function
The audit trigger does not write an actor_id that no longer exists (skip the audit row on cascade-delete, or drop the FK to ON DELETE SET NULL semantics that apply at insert time)
An erased account leaves no rows in leads, listings, testimonials, user_settings, article_webhooks or analytics_views — verified by counting them after the delete
Foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE exist on the tenant tables that lack them, added NOT VALID first if production may hold orphans
The audit trail of the deletion itself survives the deletion (an erasure record with a null actor is fine; losing the record is not)
npm run verify:schema passes
userStories.notes: DONE 2026-08-08 in migration 20260808000006_fix_account_deletion.sql. Two defects. (1) The DELETE aborted: deleting auth.users cascades to profiles, the audit trigger fires, audit_table_change() finds auth.uid() NULL under the cron caller and falls back to the row's own id, and log_audit_event() then inserts that as user_id/actor_id — referencing an auth.users row already removed in the same statement. ON DELETE SET NULL on audit_logs does not help, because the row is being INSERTED with a dangling reference rather than updated to one. log_audit_event now nulls either id when the referenced user is gone, so the erasure RECORD survives while the reference does not — losing the audit trail of a deletion would be worse than losing the actor on it. (2) leads, listings, testimonials, user_settings, article_webhooks and analytics_views carried a user_id with no foreign key at all, so nothing cascaded to them even once the delete worked. Added ON DELETE CASCADE, NOT VALID: production may hold orphans from before this and a validating ADD CONSTRAINT would fail on them, while NOT VALID still enforces on new rows and still cascades, which is what erasure needs. Sweep orphans and VALIDATE as a follow-up. account_deletion_log deliberately gets no cascading FK — it has to outlive the user. Verified end to end on a rebuilt Postgres by seeding a user with a profile, lead, listing, testimonial, settings row and analytics row and running the exact DELETE the scheduler runs: it now succeeds (previously an FK error), every one of those counts goes to 0, and 3 audit rows survive with actor_id nulled.
